Even though the runtime bundles many libraries, you can add more at the cluster level by installing PyPI, Maven, or CRAN packages, or by uploading wheels and JARs, and at the notebook level with commands like %pip install. For reproducibility, teams often pin library versions in cluster configuration or use init scripts, so every run gets the same dependencies rather than relying on ad hoc installs.

followUps.question: How does the runtime relate to open-source Spark versions?
followUps.answer: Each Databricks Runtime is built on a specific Apache Spark version but is not identical to it; Databricks applies performance optimizations, backports fixes, and bundles Delta Lake and other components. So a runtime might be based on Spark 3.5 but include enhancements not present in the vanilla 3.5 release. When checking feature availability, you generally look at the runtime version's release notes rather than only the underlying Spark version.

question: What are Databricks Repos and how does Git integration work?
directAnswer: Databricks Repos are special workspace folders linked to an external Git provider like GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, or Bitbucket. They bring proper version control into Databricks, so you can clone a repository, create branches, commit, pull, and push directly from the workspace. This lets notebook and code development follow the same branching, review, and CI/CD practices as regular software engineering.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A Repo is a Git-backed folder in the Databricks workspace. Instead of relying only on the workspace's lightweight revision history, the contents are a working copy of a real Git repository, with full branch and commit operations available through the UI and APIs.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Treating notebooks as untracked files in a workspace makes collaboration, code review, and promotion to production fragile. Repos exist to apply mature software engineering practices, version control, branching, pull requests, and CI/CD, to data and ML code, so teams can develop reliably and deploy with confidence.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You connect Databricks to a Git provider using a personal access token or app integration, then clone a repo into the Repos area. You work on a branch, edit notebooks and files, commit and push from the Git panel, and open pull requests in the provider for review. Notebooks are stored in a source-friendly format so diffs are meaningful. For deployment, CI/CD tools or Databricks Asset Bundles pull a specific commit or branch into the target workspace and run it.

whyImportant: Modern data teams are expected to apply software engineering discipline, and Repos are how that happens in Databricks. Interviewers ask this to confirm you can work with version control and reason about promoting code from dev to prod cleanly.
realWorldExample: A team develops a pipeline on a feature branch in a Repo, opens a pull request on GitHub for review, and after approval merges to main. Their CI/CD pipeline then deploys main into the production workspace and triggers a job, so the exact reviewed code runs in production rather than someone manually copying notebooks.

nestedTopics.title: Branching workflow
nestedTopics.explanation: Within a Repo you create feature branches, commit changes, and switch branches just like local Git. This enables parallel work and safe experimentation, with main kept clean for production, mirroring standard developer workflows inside the Databricks UI.

nestedTopics.title: Notebook source format
nestedTopics.explanation: Databricks stores notebooks in a text-based source format in Git, so commits produce readable diffs rather than opaque binary changes. This makes code review of notebook changes practical, which is essential for trustworthy collaboration.

nestedTopics.title: CI/CD and deployment
nestedTopics.explanation: Repos integrate with CI/CD tooling and Databricks Asset Bundles to promote code across environments. A pipeline can check out a specific commit into a workspace and deploy jobs from it, ensuring the deployed artifact matches exactly what was reviewed and tested.

followUps.question: How is a Repo different from the workspace's built-in revision history?
followUps.answer: The workspace's built-in revision history is a simple, automatic snapshot trail of a single notebook within Databricks, useful for casual undo but not real version control. A Repo connects to an external Git provider and gives full Git features: branches, commits, merges, pull requests, and integration with the team's wider codebase and CI/CD. For any serious collaboration or production promotion, Repos are the right tool, while revision history is just a lightweight safety net.

followUps.question: How do you authenticate Databricks with a Git provider?
followUps.answer: You configure Git credentials in your user settings, typically a personal access token from the provider, or use an app-based integration where supported. Databricks uses those credentials to clone, pull, and push on your behalf. For automation and team setups, organizations often use service principals with their own Git credentials so deployment pipelines can interact with the repository without depending on an individual's personal token.

followUps.question: Can you run a job directly from code in a Repo?
followUps.answer: Yes. Job tasks can point at a notebook or script inside a Repo and even at a specific Git branch, tag, or commit. This means production jobs run the exact versioned code rather than a copy stored loosely in the workspace, which improves reproducibility and traceability. Combined with CI/CD, you can ensure that what runs in production always corresponds to a reviewed, committed state in version control.

question: What are Databricks Jobs and why are they used?
directAnswer: A Databricks Job is a way to run code automatically on a schedule or trigger, rather than manually in a notebook. A job runs one or more tasks, such as a notebook, a script, a SQL query, or a JAR, usually on a dedicated job cluster, and Databricks handles scheduling, retries, alerting, and monitoring. Jobs are how you move from interactive development to reliable, automated production pipelines.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A Job is a defined unit of automated work in Databricks. In its simplest form it runs a single notebook on a schedule, and in more advanced form it orchestrates multiple dependent tasks as a workflow. Each run is tracked with status, logs, and metrics.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Running notebooks by hand does not scale and is unreliable for production: someone has to remember to run them, handle failures, and check results. Jobs exist to automate execution with proper scheduling, isolated compute, automatic retries, and notifications, so pipelines run dependably without human babysitting.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You create a job, define its tasks, and choose compute, typically a job cluster that spins up for the run and terminates after. You set a trigger, such as a cron-like schedule, file arrival, or manual or API start, and configure retries and alerts. When triggered, Databricks provisions the cluster, runs the tasks in dependency order, records each run with logs and status, and notifies you on success or failure. You monitor everything from the Workflows UI.

whyImportant: Automation is the difference between a prototype and a production data platform. Interviewers ask about Jobs to confirm you know how to operationalize notebooks with scheduling, isolation, retries, and monitoring.
realWorldExample: A nightly job is scheduled to run at 2 AM. It spins up a job cluster, runs an ingestion notebook, then a transformation notebook, then a data-quality check, retries up to two times on transient failures, and emails the team if it fails. The cluster terminates afterward, so the company gets a reliable daily pipeline at minimal cost.

nestedTopics.title: Tasks
nestedTopics.explanation: A task is a single step in a job, such as running a notebook, a Python script, a SQL query, a dbt project, or a JAR. A job can contain one task or many, and tasks are the building blocks you wire together into a workflow.

nestedTopics.title: Triggers and schedules
nestedTopics.explanation: Jobs run on triggers: a time-based schedule using cron syntax, file-arrival triggers, continuous triggers for streaming, or manual and API starts. The trigger determines when the automation kicks off, decoupling execution from human action.

nestedTopics.title: Retries and alerts
nestedTopics.explanation: Jobs can automatically retry failed tasks a configured number of times to handle transient errors, and they can send notifications on start, success, or failure via email or integrations. These features make automated pipelines resilient and observable.

followUps.question: What is the difference between a job and a notebook run?
followUps.answer: A notebook run is an interactive, manual execution you watch in the browser, suited to development. A job is an automated, managed execution: it runs on a schedule or trigger, typically on a dedicated job cluster, with retries, alerting, parameter passing, and run history. The same notebook can be run interactively during development and then wrapped in a job for production, where it executes reliably without anyone present.

followUps.question: What compute should a job use?
followUps.answer: Production jobs should generally use a job cluster, which Databricks creates fresh for the run and tears down afterward. This gives isolation, reproducibility, and lower cost since job compute is billed at a cheaper tier only for the run's duration. Running jobs on a shared all-purpose cluster is possible but costs more and risks contention. For latency-sensitive, frequently running jobs, instance pools can speed up the cluster startup.

followUps.question: How do you pass parameters to a job?
followUps.answer: You define parameters on the job or task, and they are passed into the notebook through widgets or into a script as arguments. For example, a job can supply a run_date parameter that the notebook reads with dbutils.widgets.get('run_date'). This lets the same code run for different dates or inputs across runs, and you can also override parameters when triggering a run manually or via the API for backfills and one-off executions.

question: What are the different personas in Databricks and how do they collaborate?
directAnswer: Databricks is built for several personas, primarily data engineers, data analysts, data scientists, and ML engineers, plus platform administrators. Each has a tailored experience: engineers build pipelines, analysts run SQL and dashboards, scientists train models, and ML engineers deploy them. They collaborate by all reading and writing the same governed Delta tables, so there is one shared source of truth instead of siloed copies.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Personas describe the roles Databricks serves, each with workflows and UI experiences suited to their work. The platform exposes focused experiences, such as Data Science and Engineering, Databricks SQL, and Machine Learning, while keeping a common data and governance foundation underneath.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Traditionally these roles used separate tools and separate data copies, causing inconsistency, duplicated effort, and friction handing work between teams. Databricks unifies them so they collaborate on shared data with shared governance, reducing the gaps where data and definitions diverge between teams.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Engineers ingest and transform raw data into clean Delta tables using notebooks and jobs. Analysts query those tables in Databricks SQL to build dashboards and reports. Data scientists use the same tables to train models, tracking experiments with MLflow. ML engineers operationalize models for serving. Unity Catalog governs who can access what across all of them, and because everyone works on the same tables, a metric defined once is consistent everywhere.

whyImportant: Understanding personas shows you grasp Databricks as a collaboration platform, not just a Spark runner. Interviewers value candidates who can describe how a dataset flows from engineering to analytics to ML on one platform.
realWorldExample: A data engineer builds a curated customer table. An analyst uses it to report on retention in a dashboard, while a data scientist trains a churn model on the very same table. When the engineer fixes a data-quality issue, both the dashboard and the model benefit automatically, because they share one governed source rather than separate extracts.

nestedTopics.title: Data engineer
nestedTopics.explanation: Builds and maintains ingestion and transformation pipelines, often with notebooks, Jobs, Auto Loader, and Delta Live Tables, producing reliable curated tables. They focus on reliability, performance, and data quality of the pipelines feeding everyone else.

nestedTopics.title: Data analyst
nestedTopics.explanation: Works mostly in Databricks SQL, writing queries, building dashboards, and setting alerts on curated tables. They turn governed data into business insight and typically do not need Spark or Python, just SQL.

nestedTopics.title: Data scientist and ML engineer
nestedTopics.explanation: Data scientists explore data and train models, tracking runs with MLflow, while ML engineers deploy and monitor those models in production. Both rely on the same governed tables, ensuring models are trained on the same trusted data analysts report on.

followUps.question: How does sharing the same tables prevent inconsistency?
followUps.answer: When analysts, engineers, and scientists all query the same governed Delta tables, a business metric like active users is defined and computed from one place. There are no divergent extracts where one team's number drifts from another's. A fix or improvement to the underlying table propagates to everyone at once. This shared source of truth is a core benefit of the lakehouse, eliminating the classic problem of dashboards and models disagreeing because they used different data copies.

followUps.question: Do all personas use notebooks?
followUps.answer: Not necessarily. Engineers and data scientists live in notebooks, but analysts often work entirely in the Databricks SQL editor and dashboards, never opening a notebook. Administrators work in admin and account consoles. Databricks deliberately offers role-appropriate interfaces so each persona uses the experience that fits their skills, while everyone's work still rests on the same data and governance layer underneath.

followUps.question: What does a Databricks administrator do?
followUps.answer: Administrators manage the platform rather than build pipelines. They handle users and groups, configure workspaces, set cluster policies to control cost, manage Unity Catalog metastores and permissions, oversee security and networking, and monitor usage and spend. Their job is to provide a secure, well-governed, cost-controlled environment so the other personas can work safely and efficiently. Strong admin practices are what keep a multi-team Databricks deployment healthy.

question: What collaborative features does Databricks provide?
directAnswer: Databricks is built for teamwork. Its main collaborative features are real-time co-editing of notebooks like Google Docs, inline comments, notebook revision history, sharing with fine-grained permissions, Git-based Repos for version control, and shared compute and data. Together these let teams develop, review, and operate data work together rather than passing files around.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Collaboration in Databricks spans editing, reviewing, version control, and shared resources. Multiple people can edit the same notebook simultaneously, leave comments, see who changed what, and share notebooks, dashboards, clusters, and tables with controlled access.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Data and ML work is rarely solo; engineers, analysts, and scientists must build on each other's work. Without collaboration features, teams resort to emailing notebooks and copying data, which causes version drift and lost work. These features exist to make working together smooth and traceable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Notebooks support live multi-user editing with visible cursors, and you can attach comments to specific cells for discussion. Built-in revision history records changes so you can review or revert, while Repos add full Git workflows for serious version control. Permissions on notebooks, folders, clusters, jobs, and Unity Catalog objects control who can view, run, edit, or manage each asset. Shared clusters and shared governed tables mean teams literally work on the same resources.

whyImportant: Collaboration is one of Databricks' core selling points over running Spark yourself. Interviewers ask this to see you appreciate the platform as a team environment and know the mechanisms that keep shared work organized and safe.
realWorldExample: Two engineers pair on a tricky transformation, co-editing the same notebook in real time while discussing through inline comments. A reviewer later checks the revision history to see exactly what changed, and because the notebook lives in a Repo, the final version goes through a pull request before reaching production.

nestedTopics.title: Real-time co-editing and comments
nestedTopics.explanation: Multiple users can edit a notebook simultaneously, seeing each other's cursors and changes live, and can attach comments to cells. This turns notebooks into a shared workspace for pairing, discussion, and review without exporting or emailing files.

nestedTopics.title: Revision history vs Repos
nestedTopics.explanation: Built-in revision history gives an automatic, lightweight change log per notebook for quick undo and review. Repos provide full Git version control with branches and pull requests for rigorous, team-wide versioning. Teams use the former for convenience and the latter for production-grade control.

nestedTopics.title: Permissions and sharing
nestedTopics.explanation: Access control lists on notebooks, folders, clusters, and jobs, plus Unity Catalog grants on data, let you share precisely, granting view, run, edit, or manage rights as appropriate. This makes collaboration safe by ensuring people only access what they should.

followUps.question: How do comments help in a notebook?
followUps.answer: Inline comments let teammates discuss specific cells without altering the code, which is ideal for reviews and questions. A reviewer can flag a line that needs attention, the author can respond, and the thread stays attached to the relevant cell. This keeps conversation in context rather than scattered across chat or email, making notebook review more like a code review and improving the quality and traceability of collaborative work.

followUps.question: Can you control who can run versus only view a notebook?
followUps.answer: Yes. Notebook permissions are graded: Can Read lets someone view but not execute, Can Run allows execution, Can Edit allows changing the code, and Can Manage allows changing permissions too. This granularity lets you, for example, share a notebook so stakeholders can read results without being able to run or modify it, while teammates get edit access. Managing these via groups keeps it scalable across many people.

followUps.question: How do teams avoid stepping on each other in shared clusters?
followUps.answer: Shared all-purpose clusters let several people develop on the same compute, but heavy work by one user can slow others. Teams manage this with cluster policies, separate clusters for heavy jobs, and using job clusters for production so interactive and automated work do not collide. For SQL, multi-cluster SQL Warehouses scale out to handle concurrency. The general practice is to keep exploratory work on shared interactive compute and isolate heavy or production work.

question: What is a DBU and how does Databricks pricing work at a high level?
directAnswer: A DBU, or Databricks Unit, is the unit Databricks uses to measure processing consumption. You are billed in DBUs based on the compute you use, with the DBU rate varying by workload type and features, for example all-purpose compute costs more per DBU than jobs compute, and Photon-enabled and Serverless options have their own rates. On top of DBUs you also pay your cloud provider for the underlying VMs in the classic model.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A DBU is a normalized measure of compute consumption per unit time. Your Databricks bill is essentially the number of DBUs consumed multiplied by a per-DBU price that depends on the compute type, tier, and cloud. It is how Databricks meters usage independent of raw VM hours.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different workloads and features deliver different value and cost, so a flat VM-hour price would not reflect that. DBUs exist to price consumption in a consistent, workload-aware way, letting Databricks charge more for premium experiences like all-purpose interactive compute or Serverless and less for batch jobs compute.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each cluster or warehouse consumes DBUs at a rate determined by its size and type while it runs. The same node running an all-purpose workload bills more DBUs-equivalent cost than running a job, because the per-DBU price is higher for all-purpose. Photon and Serverless carry their own rates. In the classic model you separately pay the cloud provider for the VMs; with Serverless the compute cost is folded into a single Databricks charge. This is why cost control centers on right-sizing, auto-termination, and using job clusters.

whyImportant: Cost awareness is a practical expectation for data engineers. Interviewers ask about DBUs to confirm you understand what drives spend, so your design choices, like job versus all-purpose clusters and auto-termination, are cost-conscious.
realWorldExample: A team notices its bill is high because production pipelines run on an always-on all-purpose cluster. They move the pipelines to job clusters that terminate after each run, enable aggressive auto-termination on the dev cluster, and the DBU consumption, and thus the bill, drops significantly because they stop paying the higher all-purpose rate around the clock.

nestedTopics.title: Compute tiers and DBU rates
nestedTopics.explanation: All-purpose compute has a higher per-DBU price than jobs compute, reflecting interactive convenience versus batch automation. Choosing the right tier for the workload is one of the biggest levers on cost, which is why production runs belong on job clusters.

nestedTopics.title: DBUs plus cloud cost
nestedTopics.explanation: In the classic model your total cost is Databricks DBUs plus the cloud provider's VM charges. So a cluster's expense has two components, and reducing either, fewer or smaller nodes, less runtime, lowers the bill. Serverless bundles these into one Databricks charge.

nestedTopics.title: Cost controls
nestedTopics.explanation: Auto-termination, autoscaling, cluster policies, instance pools, and using Serverless scale-to-zero are the practical tools to manage DBU consumption. Good design keeps compute running only as long as needed and sized to the workload.

followUps.question: Why is all-purpose compute more expensive than jobs compute?
followUps.answer: All-purpose compute is priced higher per DBU because it is meant for interactive, shared, always-available development, which is a more flexible and convenient mode. Jobs compute is for automated, isolated batch runs and is priced lower to encourage running production workloads there. The practical takeaway is that running production pipelines on all-purpose clusters wastes money, and moving them to job clusters both lowers the rate and limits runtime to just the job's duration.

followUps.question: How does auto-termination save money?
followUps.answer: Auto-termination shuts down a cluster after a set period of inactivity, so a forgotten or idle cluster stops consuming DBUs and cloud VM hours instead of running all night. Since you pay for compute as long as it is up regardless of whether it is doing work, idle time is pure waste. Setting a sensible auto-termination window, for example 20 to 30 minutes, is one of the simplest and most effective cost controls for interactive clusters.

followUps.question: Does Serverless cost more or less than classic compute?
followUps.answer: It depends on the workload. Serverless can cost more per unit of compute because Databricks manages the infrastructure and you pay a premium for instant startup and elasticity. But it can also save money overall by eliminating idle time through fast scale-up and scale-to-zero, and by avoiding paying for slow-starting clusters that sit warm waiting for work. For spiky, interactive, or intermittent workloads, Serverless often nets out cheaper despite a higher per-unit rate.

question: How do you read and write data in Databricks using Spark?
directAnswer: You read data with spark.read, specifying a format and path, and write it with DataFrame.write, specifying a format and mode. The default and recommended format is Delta. For example, df = spark.read.format('delta').load(path) reads a Delta table, and df.write.format('delta').mode('overwrite').saveAsTable('catalog.schema.table') writes one. You can also read common formats like CSV, JSON, and Parquet the same way.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Reading and writing data is the core I/O of Spark in Databricks. The DataFrameReader (spark.read) loads data from storage into a DataFrame, and the DataFrameWriter (df.write) persists a DataFrame back to storage or a table, with options controlling format, schema handling, and write behavior.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Every pipeline ingests data, transforms it, and writes results. A consistent, format-agnostic API exists so you can read from many sources and write to many targets with the same patterns, while Delta provides the reliable default for the lakehouse.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: For reading, you choose a format, set options like header or schema, and provide a path or table name: spark.read.format('csv').option('header', 'true').load(path) or spark.read.table('catalog.schema.table'). For writing, you set a format and a save mode, such as overwrite, append, or errorIfExists, then call save(path) for a path or saveAsTable(name) to register it in the catalog. With Delta, writes go through the transaction log, giving ACID guarantees automatically.

whyImportant: Basic read and write is the first thing you do in any Databricks task, so fluency is assumed. Interviewers check that you know the Delta default, save modes, and the difference between writing to a path versus a managed table.
realWorldExample: An ingestion notebook reads raw CSV files with spark.read.format('csv').option('header','true').load('/Volumes/main/bronze/raw'), cleans the DataFrame, and writes a curated Delta table with df.write.format('delta').mode('append').saveAsTable('main.silver.customers'), so downstream analysts query a reliable, governed table rather than raw files.

nestedTopics.title: Save modes
nestedTopics.explanation: mode('overwrite') replaces existing data, mode('append') adds to it, mode('errorIfExists') fails if the target exists, and mode('ignore') silently skips if it exists. Choosing the right mode controls whether a write replaces, extends, or guards existing data.

nestedTopics.title: save vs saveAsTable
nestedTopics.explanation: save(path) writes files to a storage location without registering them in the catalog, while saveAsTable(name) writes the data and registers it as a managed or external table in the metastore. saveAsTable makes the data queryable by name and governed by Unity Catalog, which is usually what you want.

nestedTopics.title: Reading common formats
nestedTopics.explanation: spark.read.format supports delta, parquet, csv, json, and more, with options like header, inferSchema, and an explicit schema. Delta is preferred for managed data, while CSV and JSON are common for raw ingestion before conversion to Delta.

followUps.question: Why specify a schema instead of using inferSchema?
followUps.answer: inferSchema makes Spark scan the data to guess column types, which costs an extra pass over the data and can guess wrong, for example reading a ZIP code as an integer and dropping leading zeros. Providing an explicit schema is faster because it skips the inference pass and is safer because types are exactly what you intend. For production ingestion, defining the schema explicitly avoids both the performance hit and subtle data-corruption bugs that inference can introduce.

followUps.question: What is the difference between load(path) and table(name)?
followUps.answer: load(path) reads data directly from a storage location, so you must know the physical path and you get raw files with no catalog governance. table(name) or spark.read.table reads a table registered in the catalog by its catalog.schema.table name, which is governed by Unity Catalog permissions and decouples your code from physical paths. Referencing tables by name is preferred because it is governed, portable, and lets storage move without breaking your code.

followUps.question: How do you handle writing to a partitioned Delta table?
followUps.answer: You use partitionBy when writing, for example df.write.format('delta').partitionBy('event_date').saveAsTable('events'), which organizes data into directories by the partition column so queries filtering on it can skip irrelevant data. Partitioning helps for large tables filtered on a low-cardinality column like date. However, over-partitioning on high-cardinality columns creates too many tiny files and hurts performance, so on Delta many teams rely on liquid clustering or ZORDER instead of heavy manual partitioning.

question: What is the difference between a DataFrame and a table in Databricks?
directAnswer: A DataFrame is an in-memory, distributed collection of data within a Spark session, like a logical view of data you are processing in code; it disappears when the session ends unless you persist it. A table is a persisted, named dataset registered in the catalog and backed by files in storage, available to anyone with access across sessions. You read a table into a DataFrame to process it and write a DataFrame out to a table to persist it.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A DataFrame is the core Spark programming abstraction: a distributed dataset with a schema that you transform with operations like select, filter, join, and aggregate. A table is a catalog object, managed or external, that points at durable data in storage and is referenced by a three-level name in Unity Catalog.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: You need both a working representation for computation and a durable, shareable representation for storage and governance. DataFrames exist for flexible in-code processing, while tables exist to persist results, give them a stable name, and govern access, so the two serve different stages of the data lifecycle.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: DataFrames are lazy: transformations build a plan that only executes when an action like count or write runs, and the results live in the cluster's memory and disk during the session. Tables live in the metastore as definitions pointing at Delta files in storage; they persist independently of any cluster. You convert between them with spark.read.table to load a table into a DataFrame and df.write.saveAsTable to persist a DataFrame as a table. Temp views are a middle ground: SQL-queryable names that exist only for the session.

whyImportant: Confusing DataFrames with tables is a common beginner mistake. Interviewers ask this to confirm you understand which data is ephemeral versus persisted and governed, which matters for correctness and for designing pipelines.
realWorldExample: An engineer loads the orders table into a DataFrame, joins it with customers, and computes a summary. The summary DataFrame only exists in memory during the run, so they call saveAsTable('main.gold.order_summary') to persist it as a governed table that the BI team can query the next morning, long after the cluster has shut down.

nestedTopics.title: Lazy evaluation
nestedTopics.explanation: DataFrame transformations are not executed immediately; Spark builds a logical plan and only runs it when an action is triggered. This lets Spark optimize the whole plan before executing, but it also means a DataFrame is a recipe for computation, not stored results, until you persist it.

nestedTopics.title: Managed vs external tables
nestedTopics.explanation: A managed table has both its data and metadata managed by the catalog, so dropping it deletes the data. An external table's metadata is in the catalog but its data lives at a path you control, so dropping it removes only the registration. Tables are durable either way, unlike DataFrames.

nestedTopics.title: Temporary views
nestedTopics.explanation: createOrReplaceTempView registers a DataFrame as a SQL-queryable name for the current session only. It is not a persisted table; it vanishes when the session ends and is not governed by the catalog, making it a convenient bridge between DataFrame and SQL during development.

followUps.question: If I compute a DataFrame, is the result saved anywhere?
followUps.answer: No, not automatically. A DataFrame is just a logical plan plus, after an action, results held in cluster memory and spill for that session. Once the cluster terminates or the session ends, that result is gone. To save it you must explicitly write it, for example with saveAsTable or write to a path. This is why beginners are surprised when results vanish: persistence is always an explicit step in Spark, never implicit.

followUps.question: What is the difference between a temp view and a table?
followUps.answer: A temporary view is a session-scoped name over a DataFrame that lets you query it with SQL, but it is not stored, not governed, and disappears when the session ends. A table is persisted in the catalog, backed by durable files, governed by permissions, and available across sessions and to other users. Use a temp view for convenience during a single notebook run, and create a real table when you need the data to survive and be shared.

followUps.question: Does caching a DataFrame make it a table?
followUps.answer: No. df.cache() or df.persist() keeps the DataFrame's computed results in cluster memory or disk to speed up repeated access within the session, but it does not persist the data durably or register it in the catalog. The cache lives only on that cluster for that session and is lost when the cluster stops. Caching is a performance optimization, not a persistence mechanism, so to truly save data you still must write it to a table or files.
